---
title: "F4 · Evaluation as architecture"
description: "Every step from version 0 to the final design needs evidence. Evaluation is the component that produces it."
---

In classic systems you can reason about correctness: the cache returns what was stored, the
queue delivers at least once. A model does not let you do that. It will be right on most inputs,
wrong on some, and you will not know which until you check. So evaluation is not a phase at the end
of the project. It is a component of the architecture, built before version 1, and every "where it
breaks" section in this book starts with its output.

## Three layers of checks

| Layer | What it checks | Cost | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deterministic | Structure and hard rules | Free, instant | Output parses as JSON; every citation ID exists; the SQL is read-only; the answer is under 200 words |
| Reference-based | Agreement with a known answer | Cheap | Extracted invoice total equals the labelled total; the right document is in the top 5 |
| Judged | Qualities a rule cannot capture | A model call per example, or a person's time | Is the answer correct and fully supported by the sources? Is the tone right? |

Use them in that order. A deterministic check that catches 10% of failures for free beats a model
judge that catches the same 10% for money. Most teams under-use the first layer.

## Component and end-to-end

Measure each stage separately as well as the whole. In a retrieval system, if the answer is wrong,
the cause is either that retrieval missed the right passage or that the model misused a passage it
had. Those need different fixes. So you measure **retrieval recall** (was the right passage in what
we gave the model?) separately from **faithfulness** (did the answer use only what it was given?)
and **correctness** (is the answer right?). [System 7](../systems/07-simple-rag.qmd) shows the
pattern; nearly every system has an equivalent split.

## The golden set

A golden set is a list of inputs with what a good output looks like: a reference answer, the
document that should be retrieved, the label, or a rubric. Three rules:

1. **Real inputs.** Pull them from logs, tickets, chat history or the future users. Invented
   examples are cleaner than reality and will flatter the system.
2. **Stratified.** Include the hard and rare cases on purpose: ambiguous questions, questions with
   no answer in the data, adversarial inputs, other languages. Tag each example with its category
   so you can see which category broke.
3. **Versioned.** Store it in the repository, change it through review, and never tune prompts on
   the examples you report scores on. Keep a held-out slice.

### How big

A score on $n$ examples has a standard error of $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. At an accuracy around 80%:

::: {.numbers}
n = 100   standard error 4.0 points   95% interval +/- 7.8 points
n = 200   standard error 2.8 points   95% interval +/- 5.5 points
n = 400   standard error 2.0 points   95% interval +/- 3.9 points
n = 800   standard error 1.4 points   95% interval +/- 2.8 points
:::

So with 200 examples, a change from 80% to 84% is inside the noise. Two things help. Compare
systems **on the same examples** and count only the examples where they disagree (a paired test
needs far fewer examples than comparing two independent scores). And grow the set over time from
production failures; a golden set that only grows is a regression suite.

## Model as judge

When a property needs judgement, a model can grade it. It works, if you treat the judge as a
component that also needs evaluating.

- **Prefer pairwise to absolute.** "Which of these two answers is better?" is more reliable than
  "score this answer from 1 to 10".
- **Known biases.** Judges prefer the first answer shown (randomise order), longer answers (tell
  them length is not a criterion), and answers written by their own model family (use a judge
  from a different family where it matters).
- **Calibrate against people.** Have two people label 100 examples. Measure agreement between them
  and between each of them and the judge, using Cohen's kappa. If the judge agrees with people
  about as well as people agree with each other (kappa of 0.6 or more is a reasonable bar), use it.
  If not, fix the rubric before trusting any number it produces.
- **Give it a rubric, not a vibe.** "Correct means every factual claim in the answer appears in
  the sources and none contradicts them" is gradeable. "Is this a good answer?" is not.

Judging costs money. A 500-example run where each judgement reads 3,000 tokens and writes 200,
on a workhorse model, is about 1.5M input and 100K output tokens: a few dollars per run. Cheap
enough to run on every pull request that touches a prompt.

## Evaluation in the delivery pipeline

Treat prompts, model versions, retrieval settings and tool definitions as code. A change to any
of them runs the evaluation in CI on the same examples as the last release, and the gate is
paired: count the examples that passed before and fail now, and fail the build if that count is
above a threshold you set in advance. Comparing two overall scores against the noise level hides a
change that fixes five examples and breaks five others. Report the count of examples evaluated
with the result, and fail if the count is zero: an evaluation that examined nothing did not pass.

## Online signals

The golden set tells you about the cases you thought of. Production tells you about the rest.

| Signal | What it means | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Explicit feedback (thumbs) | Direct, but rare | Under 2% of users click; skewed towards the annoyed |
| Task completion | Did the user do the thing after the answer? | Needs product instrumentation |
| Escalation or handoff rate | How often the system gave up or the user asked for a person | The single best health metric for support systems |
| Reformulation rate | User asked again in different words within a minute | Strong sign the first answer missed |
| Refusal rate | System said "I don't know" | Too low is as worrying as too high |

Sample production traffic into a review queue every week, label it, and add the failures to the
golden set. This loop, more than any model upgrade, is what makes systems better over time.
